svg.text: The final common path: from motor neuron to force
Motor-unit recruitment and firing rates are continuously transformed by muscle–tendon mechanics.
One motor unit—and two forms of motor output
α motor neurons activate extrafusal fibers; γ motor neurons adjust muscle-spindle sensitivity.
CONVERGENT INPUT TO THE MOTOR-NEURON POOL

text.tspan: “owns” a motor unit or an entire muscle.

svg.text: One highlighted α motor neuron + the extrafusal fibers it innervates = one motor unit
Motor-unit fibers are intermingled with fibers belonging to other units.
α motor axon + highlighted motor unit
fibers belonging to other motor units
Recruitment and rate coding act together
As force demand rises, active units fire faster while additional units enter the pool.

text.tspan: Smaller, fatigue-resistant units generally enter before larger, more forceful units.
Size ordering is a strong tendency—not an immutable sequence.

svg.text: The same motor-pool output can produce different force
Identical units are recruited at identical firing rates; the mechanical context changes.
same units recruited; same firing rates
Illustrative mechanical contexts—not a universal quantitative ranking.

text.tspan: Length, velocity, activation history, tendon compliance, joint geometry, co-contraction,
and external load transform motor-neuron output into force and movement.

svg.text: Lower motor neurons are the final neural bottleneck. The mechanical body determines what that output physically accomplishes.
